teaser: Sign in with Google says who you are; a passkey's PRF bytes derive a door vault, which opens your master vault. No key is stored anywhere.
core_idea: An end-to-end, client-side account with no sign-in, no account and no email: a passkey with the WebAuthn PRF extension for 32 bytes only the user's authenticator can produce for the site, and sgit vaults. Because sgit vault keys are made in the client, the browser derives a door vault's key and id from the PRF bytes with HKDF, so nothing has to be stored or found first; the door holds the master vault key, and the master holds the keys of the user's other vaults, the access key, a key pair and the list of doors. A 128-bit recovery code derives a recovery door. Google holds no key; Drive's app-data folder can keep a backup. PRF works in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox. The page that holds keys loads no third-party scripts. The pattern gives any static site accounts with no server and data the operator cannot read.

nodes.summary: Any static site: sign in, open your own data on any device, unreadable by the operator.

nodes.label: Where the passkey lives
nodes.summary: A synced provider or a hardware key gives every device; a clean browser gives one device plus recovery; Chrome's own store has no PRF.

quotes.text: The short answer, after the research, is that it is not kept anywhere. It is computed.
quotes.why: The answer to where the vault key lives.

quotes.text: There is no sign-in in this flow at all: the page registers a discoverable credential with a random user handle, and the only login involved is the one you already have with your passkey provider, which syncs it.
quotes.why: What the passkey needs, and what it does not.
